questions.stem: This labeled diagram depicts the layered structure of the epidermis. Why are dermatophyte infections confined to the superficial region shown here rather than invading deeper tissue?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dermatophytes are obligate intracellular organisms of basal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blood vessels in the dermis physically wall off the fungus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dermatophytes are killed instantly by melanocyte pigment

choices.label: E
choices.text: The dermis contains antifungal proteins that block invasion

explanation.summary: Dermatophytes feed on keratin found only in the stratum corneum, hair, and nails, so they remain limited to keratinized superficial layers and rarely cause deep or systemic disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dermatophytes feed on keratin found only in the stratum corneum, hair, and nails, so they remain limited to keratinized superficial layers and rarely cause deep or systemic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dermatophytes are extracellular molds that grow in keratinized dead layers, not obligate intracellular organisms of basal cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dermal blood vessels do not form a barrier walling off fungus; dermatophytes stay superficial because they depend on keratin and are inhibited by factors in living tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Melanocyte pigment does not kill dermatophytes; melanin protects against UV damage and has no direct antifungal action here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum and tissue factors such as transferrin may limit fungal growth in living tissue, but the main reason dermatophytes stay superficial is their dependence on keratin.

questions.stem: Under this ultraviolet lamp the infected area fluoresces. What is the correct interpretation of a positive and a negative result?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A negative test definitively excludes fungal infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some dermatophytes fluoresce; a negative test does NOT rule out infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: A positive test confirms bacterial infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: All dermatophytes fluoresce, so the test is fully diagnostic

explanation.summary: A Wood's lamp causes some dermatophytes (e.g., Microsporum canis) to fluoresce, but many do not, so a negative test cannot exclude a fungal infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Wood's lamp causes some dermatophytes (e.g., Microsporum canis) to fluoresce, but many do not, so a negative test cannot exclude a fungal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Wood's lamp fluorescence reflects pigments made by certain fungi or bacteria and does not indicate a viral coinfection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Many dermatophytes, including most Trichophyton species, do not fluoresce, so a negative test cannot exclude fungal infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Some bacteria fluoresce, such as Corynebacterium minutissimum in erythrasma with coral-red color, but fluorescence does not confirm a bacterial cause by itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only some dermatophytes, mainly certain Microsporum species, fluoresce; most Trichophyton do not, so the test is not fully diagnostic.

questions.stem: This microscopy shows smooth, club/beaver-tail-shaped macroconidia in clusters with no microconidia. Which genus is this?

explanation.summary: Epidermophyton produces smooth, club-shaped macroconidia in clusters and characteristically lacks microconidia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Epidermophyton produces smooth, club-shaped macroconidia in clusters and characteristically lacks microconidia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sporothrix is a dimorphic fungus whose mold forms thin hyphae with rosette-like clusters of small conidia, not club-shaped macroconidia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malassezia is a lipophilic yeast that shows spaghetti-and-meatballs on KOH and does not produce macroconidia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trichophyton produces abundant microconidia, with macroconidia that are cigar-shaped, thin-walled, and often rare.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microsporum produces rough-walled, spindle-shaped macroconidia and some microconidia, not smooth club-shaped clusters without microconidia.

questions.stem: This microscopy shows cigar-shaped macroconidia with abundant microconidia. Which dermatophyte genus does this represent?

explanation.summary: Trichophyton is distinguished by cigar-shaped macroconidia, numerous microconidia, and sometimes coiled or spiraled hyphae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trichophyton is distinguished by cigar-shaped macroconidia, numerous microconidia, and sometimes coiled or spiraled hyphae.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Malassezia is a yeast that forms spaghetti-and-meatballs hyphae and spores, not conidia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epidermophyton has smooth club-shaped macroconidia in clusters and lacks microconidia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Microsporum has rough-walled, spindle-shaped macroconidia that are thick-walled, unlike the smooth cigar-shaped macroconidia shown.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Candida is a yeast that forms pseudohyphae and germ tubes and is not a dermatophyte with macroconidia.

questions.stem: This microscopy shows rough-walled, spindle-shaped macroconidia with microconidia present. Which genus is identified?

explanation.summary: Microsporum is identified by rough-walled, spindle-shaped macroconidia, in contrast to the smooth macroconidia of Epidermophyton.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microsporum is identified by rough-walled, spindle-shaped macroconidia, in contrast to the smooth macroconidia of Epidermophyton.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epidermophyton macroconidia are smooth and club-shaped, and microconidia are absent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sporothrix produces thin hyphae with rosettes of small conidia and lacks rough spindle-shaped macroconidia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malassezia is a lipophilic yeast seen as spaghetti-and-meatballs on KOH, without macroconidia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trichophyton macroconidia are smooth, thin-walled, and cigar-shaped, not rough-walled spindles.

questions.stem: This fungal colony is growing on the medium of choice for isolating dermatophytes. What medium is this and why is it selective?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chocolate agar, enriched for fastidious bacteria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sabouraud dextrose agar, selective due to its low pH

choices.label: D
choices.text: MacConkey agar, selective for gram-negative rods

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blood agar, selective for hemolytic organisms

explanation.summary: Sabouraud dextrose agar has a low pH (~5.6) that inhibits most bacterial growth, making it selective for fungi.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sabouraud dextrose agar has a low pH (~5.6) that inhibits most bacterial growth, making it selective for fungi.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thayer-Martin is chocolate agar with antibiotics such as vancomycin, colistin, and nystatin to select for pathogenic Neisseria; its nystatin inhibits fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chocolate agar is an enriched, nonselective medium for fastidious bacteria such as Haemophilus and Neisseria, not the fungal medium of choice.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MacConkey agar uses bile salts and crystal violet to select for gram-negative bacteria, not fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blood agar is a nonselective enriched medium used to assess hemolysis; it does not inhibit bacteria to favor fungi.

questions.stem: This KOH preparation reveals clustered round yeast cells together with short hyphal elements. What is the classic descriptive term for this appearance?

explanation.summary: Malassezia in a KOH prep shows clustered yeast cells (meatballs) with short hyphae (spaghetti), the classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Malassezia in a KOH prep shows clustered yeast cells (meatballs) with short hyphae (spaghetti), the classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An India ink halo is the clear capsule around Cryptococcus on a negative stain, not clustered yeasts with short hyphae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A chain of pearls describes nodules tracking along lymphatics in sporotrichosis, not a KOH microscopy pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sulfur granules are yellow aggregates of filamentous bacteria in Actinomyces abscesses, not yeast and short hyphae on KOH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Germ tubes are hyphal outgrowths from Candida albicans incubated in serum, not clusters of yeast mixed with short hyphae.

questions.stem: This tissue biopsy shows a central yeast surrounded by radiating, star-shaped eosinophilic material within a giant cell. What is this structure called?

explanation.summary: Asteroid bodies are star-shaped structures surrounding the yeast within giant cells of granulomas, seen in sporotrichosis, especially disseminated disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Asteroid bodies are star-shaped structures surrounding the yeast within giant cells of granulomas, seen in sporotrichosis, especially disseminated disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Psammoma bodies are laminated concentric calcifications in papillary thyroid carcinoma, meningioma, and serous ovarian tumors, not star-shaped material around yeast.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in neurons infected with rabies virus, not a radiating halo around a fungus in a giant cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Molluscum bodies are large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions in keratinocytes infected with molluscum contagiosum virus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schaumann bodies are laminated calcium and protein concretions in giant cells of sarcoidosis, not radiating material surrounding a yeast.

questions.stem: This annular skin lesion with a raised scaly advancing border and central clearing is most consistent with which condition?

explanation.summary: The classic ring shape with an active scaly border and central clearing is produced as the dermatophyte spreads outward while the immune response clears the center.
explanation.whyCorrect: The classic ring shape with an active scaly border and central clearing is produced as the dermatophyte spreads outward while the immune response clears the center.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Granuloma annulare forms annular rings of smooth skin-colored to pink papules without scale, often on the hands and feet.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythema migrans is an expanding red patch at a tick bite site, usually without the scaly advancing border of a dermatophyte infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nummular eczema forms coin-shaped, uniformly scaly or crusted plaques without central clearing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Psoriasis forms well-demarcated plaques with thick silvery scale across the whole surface, usually on extensor surfaces, not rings with central clearing.

questions.stem: This child's scalp shows a patch of hair loss with scaling and broken-off hairs. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Scaly patches with patchy alopecia and broken hairs (black dots) in a child are characteristic of dermatophyte scalp infection, tinea capitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Scaly patches with patchy alopecia and broken hairs (black dots) in a child are characteristic of dermatophyte scalp infection, tinea capitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alopecia areata causes smooth, round patches of hair loss without scale or inflammation, often with exclamation-point hairs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Trichotillomania causes irregular patches of hairs broken at varying lengths from pulling, without scale or inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seborrheic dermatitis causes greasy yellow scale on the scalp (cradle cap in infants) without patches of broken hairs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Discoid lupus causes scarring alopecia with atrophy, follicular plugging, and dyspigmentation, typically in adults rather than children.

questions.stem: This infant scalp demonstrates patchy hair loss from a dermatophyte infection. Which genera most commonly cause this presentation?

explanation.summary: Tinea capitis is most frequently caused by Trichophyton and Microsporum species; Epidermophyton does not infect hair.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tinea capitis is most frequently caused by Trichophyton and Microsporum species; Epidermophyton does not infect hair.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Malassezia causes tinea versicolor and seborrheic dermatitis, and Candida infects moist skin and mucosa; neither is a dermatophyte causing tinea capitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Staphylococcus and Streptococcus cause impetigo and folliculitis on the scalp, but they are bacteria, not dermatophytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epidermophyton infects skin and nails but not hair, and Sporothrix is a dimorphic fungus causing lymphocutaneous infection, not tinea capitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aspergillus and Fusarium are molds causing invasive infections in immunocompromised hosts or keratitis, not scalp dermatophytosis.

questions.stem: This inflamed, crusted eruption over a man's beard area is most consistent with which infection?

explanation.summary: Tinea barbae is a dermatophyte infection of the beard region, typically acquired from animals and presenting with itchy, red, crusting lesions and hair loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tinea barbae is a dermatophyte infection of the beard region, typically acquired from animals and presenting with itchy, red, crusting lesions and hair loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pseudofolliculitis barbae is an inflammatory reaction to ingrown hairs after shaving, with papules but not crusting and hair loss from infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacterial folliculitis, often S. aureus (sycosis barbae), causes follicular pustules but lacks the animal exposure and dermatophyte-associated hair loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Perioral dermatitis causes small papules around the mouth that spare the vermilion border and is often linked to topical steroids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acne vulgaris causes comedones, papules, and pustules, primarily during adolescence, not crusted beard-area lesions with hair loss.

questions.stem: This farm animal shows circular patches of hair loss with crusting from a dermatophyte. Why is recognizing this relevant to human infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It proves the infection is non-contagious to humans

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the definitive sexual host of the fungus

choices.label: E
choices.text: It shows the fungus is dimorphic only in cattle

explanation.summary: Livestock such as cattle harbor zoophilic dermatophytes (e.g., Trichophyton verrucosum) that can be transmitted to farmers and animal workers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Livestock such as cattle harbor zoophilic dermatophytes (e.g., Trichophyton verrucosum) that can be transmitted to farmers and animal workers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Zoophilic dermatophytes such as Trichophyton verrucosum readily infect humans who handle affected animals, so the animal does not prove noncontagiousness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dermatophytes do not require a definitive host for sexual reproduction, which, when it occurs, happens in the environment rather than in an animal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dermatophytes stay confined to keratinized skin and hair; ringworm lesions do not indicate systemic dissemination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dermatophytes are not dimorphic in any host; they grow as hyphae and arthroconidia in keratinized tissue.

questions.stem: This trunk lesion shows an expanding red patch with central clearing. Which organism is a particularly common cause among pet owners?

explanation.summary: Microsporum canis is a zoophilic dermatophyte commonly transmitted from cats and dogs, making it a frequent cause of tinea corporis in pet owners.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microsporum canis is a zoophilic dermatophyte commonly transmitted from cats and dogs, making it a frequent cause of tinea corporis in pet owners.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Malassezia globosa causes tinea versicolor with hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly patches, not an expanding red ring acquired from pets.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epidermophyton floccosum is anthropophilic, spread person to person and causing tinea cruris and pedis, not acquired from pets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sporothrix schenckii causes lymphocutaneous nodules after thorn injuries, though cats can transmit it; it does not cause annular tinea corporis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Candida albicans causes intertrigo with satellite pustules in moist folds, not an expanding annular plaque on the trunk.

questions.stem: This erythematous scaly eruption in the groin fold that spares the scrotum is most consistent with which condition?

explanation.summary: Tinea cruris (jock itch) affects the groin and inner thighs with an advancing scaly border and characteristically spares the scrotum, unlike candidal infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tinea cruris (jock itch) affects the groin and inner thighs with an advancing scaly border and characteristically spares the scrotum, unlike candidal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candidal intertrigo typically involves the scrotum and shows bright red macerated skin with satellite pustules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Contact dermatitis follows the shape of the irritant or allergen exposure and lacks a scaly advancing border sparing the scrotum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythrasma, caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, is a uniform brown-red patch without an active border and fluoresces coral-red under Wood's lamp.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inverse psoriasis forms smooth, sharply demarcated, glossy red plaques in folds, usually without scale or central clearing.

questions.stem: This maceration and scaling between the toes represents which form of tinea pedis?

explanation.summary: The interdigital form is the most common presentation of athlete's foot, with macerated, scaly skin predominantly between the toes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The interdigital form is the most common presentation of athlete's foot, with macerated, scaly skin predominantly between the toes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Onychomycosis involves the nails, with thickening and discoloration, not the toe-web skin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The ulcerative form is a severe extension of interdigital disease with erosions and ulcers, often with secondary bacterial infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The vesiculobullous form produces tense blisters on the instep or sole rather than maceration between toes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The moccasin form produces chronic diffuse scaling and hyperkeratosis over the sole and sides of the foot.

questions.stem: This foot shows tense blisters and erosions from a dermatophyte infection. Which form of tinea pedis is this?

explanation.summary: The vesiculobullous form presents with painful, itchy blisters on the soles that are often intensely red and swollen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vesiculobullous form presents with painful, itchy blisters on the soles that are often intensely red and swollen.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The moccasin form produces chronic diffuse dry scaling and hyperkeratosis over the soles, not tense blisters.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The interdigital form produces maceration and scaling between the toes rather than blisters on the sole.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impetigo is a bacterial infection with honey-colored crusts or flaccid bullae, not a dermatophyte infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Onychomycosis is a nail infection causing thickening and discoloration, not blisters on the foot.

questions.stem: These thickened, discolored, crumbling nails are most consistent with which condition?

explanation.summary: Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) is a dermatophyte nail infection causing thick, discolored, brittle nails that are often resistant to topical therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) is a dermatophyte nail infection causing thick, discolored, brittle nails that are often resistant to topical therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Subungual melanoma causes a longitudinal pigmented band that may spread onto the nail fold (Hutchinson sign), not thickened crumbling nails.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Psoriatic nail dystrophy shows pitting, oil-drop spots, and onycholysis, usually with skin or joint psoriasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic trauma can thicken nails but typically affects a single nail in a pattern matching the injury, without the crumbling debris of fungal infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lichen planus of the nail causes thinning, longitudinal ridging, and pterygium formation rather than thickened crumbling nails.

questions.stem: This inflamed, macerated eruption arising where two skin surfaces rub together is best described as?

explanation.summary: Intertrigo is inflammation of skin folds caused by friction, moisture, and irritation, and it can predispose to secondary bacterial and fungal infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intertrigo is inflammation of skin folds caused by friction, moisture, and irritation, and it can predispose to secondary bacterial and fungal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allergic contact dermatitis follows exposure to an allergen in a pattern matching contact, not specifically where skin rubs against skin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hidradenitis suppurativa causes painful nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts in the axillae and groin, not superficial macerated inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tinea corporis causes annular plaques with a scaly border and central clearing on the trunk or limbs, not friction-driven maceration in folds.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cellulitis is a deeper spreading bacterial infection with warmth, tenderness, and swelling, not superficial inflammation confined to skin folds.

questions.stem: This trunk shows well-demarcated patches of altered pigmentation with fine scale that became noticeable after tanning. What is the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Malassezia overgrowth causes hypo- or hyperpigmented, finely scaly patches on the trunk that become obvious after sun exposure tans the surrounding skin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Malassezia overgrowth causes hypo- or hyperpigmented, finely scaly patches on the trunk that become obvious after sun exposure tans the surrounding skin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation follows previous skin inflammation and lacks fine scale and fungal elements.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pityriasis rosea starts with a herald patch followed by oval patches in a Christmas-tree pattern, and it resolves in weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tinea corporis forms annular plaques with an active scaly border and central clearing, not patches of altered pigmentation that appear after tanning.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitiligo causes complete depigmentation from melanocyte loss, with smooth, nonscaly patches.

questions.stem: This limb shows an ulcerating nodule with additional nodules tracking proximally along the lymphatics. Which infection produces this pattern?

explanation.summary: Sporothrix schenckii inoculated through the skin produces a papule that ulcerates and spreads along lymphatic channels as a chain of nodules ('chain of pearls').
explanation.whyCorrect: Sporothrix schenckii inoculated through the skin produces a papule that ulcerates and spreads along lymphatic channels as a chain of nodules ('chain of pearls').

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nocardiosis can rarely cause lymphocutaneous spread, but it is a partially acid-fast filamentous bacterium and more often causes pulmonary or brain abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cutaneous anthrax causes a painless papule that becomes a black eschar surrounded by edema, not a chain of nodules along lymphatics.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cat-scratch disease causes a papule at the scratch site with regional lymphadenopathy, not ascending nodules along lymphatic channels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cutaneous leishmaniasis causes a chronic ulcer at a sandfly bite site; sporotrichoid spread can occur but is uncommon.

questions.stem: This household object is highlighted as a common source of dermatophyte spread. What role does it play in transmission?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a reservoir where the fungus completes sexual reproduction

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a biological vector that amplifies the fungus

choices.label: D
choices.text: It supplies the keratinase enzyme needed for infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a definitive host required for the fungal life cycle

explanation.summary: Brushes, combs, and hats are inanimate fomites that carry shed skin and hair laden with dermatophyte arthrospores, allowing indirect person-to-person transmission.
explanation.whyCorrect: Brushes, combs, and hats are inanimate fomites that carry shed skin and hair laden with dermatophyte arthrospores, allowing indirect person-to-person transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dermatophytes do not complete sexual reproduction on combs or brushes; these objects carry spores passively.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A biological vector is a living organism in which the pathogen develops or multiplies, as with mosquitoes; inanimate objects cannot amplify the fungus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Keratinase is an enzyme produced by dermatophytes themselves, not supplied by household objects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dermatophytes do not have a definitive host; they reproduce asexually by arthroconidia in keratinized tissue.

questions.stem: This diagram shows the segmented body plan of a helminth whose individual segments each contain reproductive organs. What are these segments called?

explanation.summary: Cestodes (tapeworms) have a scolex (head) and a chain of segments called proglottids; each mature proglottid is hermaphroditic, containing both male and female organs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cestodes (tapeworms) have a scolex (head) and a chain of segments called proglottids; each mature proglottid is hermaphroditic, containing both male and female organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Somites are embryonic blocks of paraxial mesoderm in vertebrates, not reproductive segments of tapeworms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Merozoites are asexual forms of Plasmodium released from hepatocytes or red cells, not helminth segments.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metameres are the repeating segments of annelids and arthropods; in tapeworms the specific term for hermaphroditic segments is proglottid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sporocysts are larval stages of trematodes that develop in snails, not segments of a cestode.

questions.stem: This electron micrograph shows a slender female worm held within a groove of the thicker male. What is this male body groove called?

explanation.summary: Adult schistosomes (blood flukes) are unusual among trematodes in having separate sexes; the male's gynecophoral canal holds the female during continuous mating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adult schistosomes (blood flukes) are unusual among trematodes in having separate sexes; the male's gynecophoral canal holds the female during continuous mating.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The acetabulum is the ventral sucker of flukes used for attachment, not the groove holding the female.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The rostellum is a projection on the scolex of some tapeworms that bears hooks, not a fluke structure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A buccal capsule is the mouth cavity of hookworms with teeth or cutting plates, not a fluke body groove.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The genital pore is the opening of the reproductive tract, not the long groove in which the female lies.

questions.stem: A skin scraping viewed under the microscope reveals this organism along with surrounding eggs. What is the diagnostic finding?

explanation.summary: Definitive diagnosis of scabies is made by scraping a burrow and identifying the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, its eggs, or fecal pellets microscopically.
explanation.whyCorrect: Definitive diagnosis of scabies is made by scraping a burrow and identifying the Sarcoptes scabiei mite, its eggs, or fecal pellets microscopically.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Louse nits are oval eggs cemented to hair shafts, found by inspecting hair, not mites with eggs in a skin-burrow scraping.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by hookworm larvae migrating in skin; diagnosis is clinical by the serpiginous track, and larvae are rarely recovered.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Demodex mites live in hair follicles and are elongated with a long tail, unlike the round Sarcoptes mite found in burrows.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Giardia trophozoites are intestinal protozoa found in stool, not skin scrapings.

questions.stem: This stool-smear organism has two nuclei and multiple flagella, giving it a face-like appearance. How does it move?

explanation.summary: Giardia lamblia is a flagellated protozoan; its paired nuclei and flagella produce the classic 'owl-face' trophozoite that causes fatty, foul-smelling diarrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: Giardia lamblia is a flagellated protozoan; its paired nuclei and flagella produce the classic 'owl-face' trophozoite that causes fatty, foul-smelling diarrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pseudopods are used by amebae such as Entamoeba histolytica, not by Giardia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Muscular body-wall contraction is how multicellular worms move; Giardia is a single-celled protozoan.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cilia propel Balantidium coli, the only ciliate pathogen of humans, not Giardia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sporozoans such as Plasmodium and Toxoplasma lack locomotor organelles, but Giardia is actively motile with flagella.

questions.stem: This large oval protozoan has a fuzzy border made of thousands of tiny structures. What is its mode of locomotion?

explanation.summary: Balantidium coli is the only ciliate known to infect humans; the fuzzy edge is thousands of cilia. It is transmitted fecal-orally and can cause dysentery.
explanation.whyCorrect: Balantidium coli is the only ciliate known to infect humans; the fuzzy edge is thousands of cilia. It is transmitted fecal-orally and can cause dysentery.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gliding motility belongs to apicomplexan sporozoites and tachyzoites; Balantidium swims rapidly with cilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An undulating membrane plus flagella is characteristic of Trichomonas and trypanosomes, not the fringe of tiny structures shown.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pseudopods are used by amebae such as Entamoeba; Balantidium is ciliated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Flagella are few and long, as in Giardia and Trichomonas, whereas the fuzzy border of thousands of short structures is cilia.

questions.stem: These intensely itchy skin findings are worst at night and cluster in finger webs and skin folds. The tunnel-like burrow lines seen are best described as:

explanation.summary: Scabies mites tunnel through the epidermis, producing serpiginous burrow lines; lesions favor finger webs, wrists, waistline, and genitals and itch worst at night.
explanation.whyCorrect: Scabies mites tunnel through the epidermis, producing serpiginous burrow lines; lesions favor finger webs, wrists, waistline, and genitals and itch worst at night.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Annular scaling plaques are the rings of tinea corporis, not linear tunnels in finger webs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vesicular dermatomal eruptions are herpes zoster, painful rather than itchy and limited to one dermatome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Petechial hemorrhagic rash reflects bleeding from thrombocytopenia or vasculitis, not mites burrowing in the epidermis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Target lesions such as erythema migrans are expanding annular patches, not short wavy burrow tunnels.

questions.stem: The arthropod shown is considered the deadliest animal on earth to humans. Why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It burrows into skin and causes an intense hypersensitivity reaction

choices.label: B
choices.text: It transmits disease only mechanically on its body surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: It multiplies within human tissue as an endoparasite

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its bite injects a directly lethal neurotoxin

choices.label: E
choices.text: It serves as a biological vector

explanation.summary: Mosquitoes are the deadliest animal to humans because they act as biological vectors, spreading malaria, arboviruses, filariasis, and other pathogens that kill millions annually.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mosquitoes are the deadliest animal to humans because they act as biological vectors, spreading malaria, arboviruses, filariasis, and other pathogens that kill millions annually.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Burrowing and causing intense hypersensitivity is the behavior of Sarcoptes scabiei mites, not mosquitoes, and is not deadly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mechanical transmission on the body surface describes houseflies carrying pathogens; mosquitoes are biological vectors in which pathogens develop.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mosquitoes feed externally and do not multiply within human tissue; endoparasites such as helminths live inside the host.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mosquito saliva contains anticoagulants and vasodilators, not a lethal neurotoxin; deaths come from the pathogens they transmit.

questions.stem: This schematic depicts a mite burrowing within the layers of host skin. What type of parasite is responsible?

explanation.summary: Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei, an ectoparasitic mite that only superficially burrows into the epidermis rather than invading deeper tissues; the itch is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei, an ectoparasitic mite that only superficially burrows into the epidermis rather than invading deeper tissues; the itch is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Protozoan endoparasites are single-celled organisms living inside the host, whereas the scabies mite is a multicellular arthropod in superficial epidermis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helminth endoparasites are worms living within internal organs or tissues, not arthropods burrowing in the stratum corneum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ciliates and flagellates are single-celled protozoa, not eight-legged arthropods.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blood flukes such as Schistosoma are trematodes living in veins, not mites in the epidermis.

questions.stem: This blood-feeding insect, much smaller than a mosquito, is the vector for which infection?

explanation.summary: Female phlebotomine sandflies transmit Leishmania spp.; mosquitoes transmit malaria and reduviid bugs transmit Chagas disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Female phlebotomine sandflies transmit Leishmania spp.; mosquitoes transmit malaria and reduviid bugs transmit Chagas disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Malaria is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes, which are larger than sandflies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: African sleeping sickness is transmitted by the tsetse fly, a large biting fly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxoplasmosis is acquired by ingesting oocysts from cat feces or tissue cysts in undercooked meat, not via an insect vector.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chagas disease is transmitted by reduviid (kissing) bugs, which deposit Trypanosoma cruzi in feces near the bite.

questions.stem: These three light-microscopy forms (cyst, ameboid, and flagellated) belong to which free-living organism responsible for a nearly always fatal CNS infection?

explanation.summary: N. fowleri uniquely exists as trophozoite, transient flagellate, and cyst forms; it causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: N. fowleri uniquely exists as trophozoite, transient flagellate, and cyst forms; it causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Trichomonas vaginalis exists only as a flagellated trophozoite with no cyst stage, and it causes vaginitis, not CNS infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Leishmania donovani alternates between amastigotes and promastigotes and causes visceral leishmaniasis, not an ameboflagellate meningoencephalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Entamoeba histolytica has trophozoite and cyst stages but no flagellated form, and it causes colitis and liver abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxoplasma gondii forms tachyzoites, bradyzoite cysts, and oocysts, none of which are flagellated or free-living amebae.

questions.stem: This tissue section shows a cyst packed with slow-dividing organisms (arrows). Which parasite forms these latent tissue cysts that reactivate with immunosuppression?

explanation.summary: T. gondii persists as bradyzoite-filled tissue cysts that reactivate when cell-mediated immunity wanes.
explanation.whyCorrect: T. gondii persists as bradyzoite-filled tissue cysts that reactivate when cell-mediated immunity wanes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Trichomonas vaginalis lives on genitourinary mucosa as trophozoites and forms no tissue cysts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leishmania donovani lives as amastigotes within macrophages of the spleen, liver, and marrow, not in latent tissue cysts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Naegleria fowleri cysts form in the environment, and the organism causes acute fatal meningoencephalitis rather than latent infection that reactivates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Giardia cysts are excreted in stool and transmit infection; Giardia does not form latent tissue cysts.

questions.stem: This Giemsa-stained CSF from a patient with rapidly progressive meningoencephalitis after freshwater swimming shows a motile trophozoite (arrow). What is the organism?

explanation.summary: Motile amebic trophozoites in CSF after warm freshwater exposure indicate N. fowleri primary amebic meningoencephalitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Motile amebic trophozoites in CSF after warm freshwater exposure indicate N. fowleri primary amebic meningoencephalitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Trypanosoma brucei is a flagellated trypomastigote transmitted by tsetse flies, causing slowly progressive sleeping sickness, not acute illness after swimming.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxoplasma causes ring-enhancing brain lesions in immunocompromised hosts and is not acquired by freshwater swimming.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acanthamoeba causes subacute to chronic granulomatous amebic encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts or keratitis in contact lens users, not rapid PAM after swimming.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast causing subacute meningitis, not a motile amebic trophozoite.

questions.stem: This head CT of an AIDS patient with a CD4 count of 75 shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Which opportunistic parasite is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in an AIDS patient are classic for reactivated cerebral toxoplasmosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in an AIDS patient are classic for reactivated cerebral toxoplasmosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Leishmania infantum causes visceral leishmaniasis with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia, not ring-enhancing brain lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Naegleria fowleri causes fulminant meningoencephalitis after freshwater exposure, not multiple ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trypanosoma cruzi causes cardiomyopathy and megaviscera; reactivation in AIDS can rarely cause brain lesions, but toxoplasmosis is far more common.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trichomonas vaginalis is a genitourinary pathogen with no CNS involvement.

questions.stem: A newborn has this non-contrast head CT showing scattered intracranial calcifications, along with chorioretinitis and hydrocephalus. Which congenital infection is most likely?

explanation.summary: The classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications points to congenital toxoplasmosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications points to congenital toxoplasmosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Congenital syphilis causes rhinitis (snuffles), skin lesions, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone changes, not chorioretinitis with hydrocephalus and diffuse calcifications.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Congenital rubella causes cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and heart defects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neonatal HSV is usually acquired at delivery and causes skin vesicles, encephalitis, or disseminated disease, not the toxoplasmosis triad.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Congenital CMV causes periventricular calcifications with microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss rather than diffuse calcifications with hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: This pear-shaped, flagellated organism seen on a saline wet mount is a common cause of which clinical picture?

choices.label: D
choices.text: A skin ulcer at a bite site

explanation.summary: The motile, pear-shaped trophozoite with an undulating membrane is T. vaginalis, which causes trichomoniasis and colpitis macularis (strawberry cervix).
explanation.whyCorrect: The motile, pear-shaped trophozoite with an undulating membrane is T. vaginalis, which causes trichomoniasis and colpitis macularis (strawberry cervix).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacterial vaginosis is a shift toward Gardnerella and anaerobes producing clue cells and fishy odor, without flagellated organisms on wet mount.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary amebic meningoencephalitis is caused by Naegleria fowleri after freshwater exposure, not a genitourinary flagellate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A skin ulcer at a bite site suggests cutaneous leishmaniasis or similar vector-borne infections, not a sexually transmitted flagellate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vulvovaginal candidiasis shows budding yeast and pseudohyphae with thick white discharge, not pear-shaped motile flagellates.

questions.stem: This wet mount shows an epithelial cell so studded with bacteria that its borders are obscured. This finding indicates infection with which organism?

explanation.summary: A clue cell (epithelial cell coated with adherent bacteria) indicates bacterial vaginosis, associated with Gardnerella vaginalis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A clue cell (epithelial cell coated with adherent bacteria) indicates bacterial vaginosis, associated with Gardnerella vaginalis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida albicans shows budding yeast and pseudohyphae on KOH, not epithelial cells coated with bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neisseria gonorrhoeae appears as intracellular gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils, not adherent bacteria on squamous cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactobacilli dominate normal vaginal flora and are depleted in bacterial vaginosis; they do not coat epithelial cells as clue cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trichomonas vaginalis appears as motile pear-shaped flagellates on wet mount, not bacteria covering epithelial cells.

questions.stem: This bone marrow smear shows a macrophage filled with small round intracellular parasites, each with a nucleus and an adjacent rod-shaped kinetoplast. What is the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Amastigotes bearing a nucleus and kinetoplast inside marrow macrophages confirm visceral leishmaniasis; Histoplasma yeasts lack a kinetoplast.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amastigotes bearing a nucleus and kinetoplast inside marrow macrophages confirm visceral leishmaniasis; Histoplasma yeasts lack a kinetoplast.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chagas disease shows amastigotes in cardiac muscle and trypomastigotes in blood, not amastigotes in marrow macrophages with this visceral picture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malaria parasites infect red blood cells, forming ring forms and schizonts, and lack a kinetoplast.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histoplasma yeasts also fill macrophages but have no kinetoplast and show a clear halo from retracted cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoplasma tachyzoites are crescent-shaped and lack a kinetoplast, and they are not typically found filling marrow macrophages.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man returning from Brazil develops this slowly enlarging, crusted ulcer with a raised border at a bug-bite site on his forearm. Which parasite is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: A painless ulcer with a raised, indurated border at a sandfly-bite site after travel to Latin America is classic cutaneous leishmaniasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A painless ulcer with a raised, indurated border at a sandfly-bite site after travel to Latin America is classic cutaneous leishmaniasis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Naegleria fowleri causes fatal meningoencephalitis after freshwater exposure, not a skin ulcer at a bite site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasmodium falciparum causes cyclic fevers and severe malaria from red cell infection, not a localized chronic skin ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Toxoplasma gondii causes lymphadenopathy or CNS and eye disease, not a crusted ulcer at a bite site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trichomonas vaginalis causes sexually transmitted vaginitis or urethritis, not skin ulcers.

questions.stem: On speculum exam this cervix shows punctate hemorrhages giving a 'strawberry' appearance, accompanied by a frothy discharge and vaginal pH above 4.5. Which organism is responsible?

explanation.summary: The strawberry cervix with frothy malodorous discharge and elevated pH is characteristic of T. vaginalis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The strawberry cervix with frothy malodorous discharge and elevated pH is characteristic of T. vaginalis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida causes thick, white, curd-like discharge with normal vaginal pH below 4.5, not frothy discharge and strawberry cervix.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chlamydia trachomatis causes mucopurulent cervicitis that is often asymptomatic, without frothy discharge or punctate cervical hemorrhages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gardnerella-associated bacterial vaginosis causes thin gray fishy discharge with pH above 4.5, but the cervix is not inflamed and no strawberry pattern is seen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes purulent cervicitis with friable cervix, not frothy discharge with punctate strawberry hemorrhages.

questions.stem: This crusted skin ulcer with a raised border developed weeks after a sandfly bite in an endemic region. Which disease does it represent?

explanation.summary: A chronic, relatively painless ulcer with a raised, rolled border at a sandfly-bite site is cutaneous leishmaniasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A chronic, relatively painless ulcer with a raised, rolled border at a sandfly-bite site is cutaneous leishmaniasis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basal cell carcinoma is a slow-growing pearly papule with rolled borders and telangiectasias in sun-exposed skin, not an ulcer after a sandfly bite.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sporotrichosis forms an ulcerating nodule with nodules ascending along lymphatics after thorn or soil inoculation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) causes fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia from systemic infection, not a localized skin ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cutaneous anthrax causes a painless black eschar with surrounding edema within days, not a chronic ulcer with a raised border weeks later.

questions.stem: This child from an endemic area has fever, wasting, and a grossly distended abdomen from massive splenomegaly ('black fever'). Which form of leishmaniasis is this?

explanation.summary: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), from L. donovani/L. infantum, causes hepatosplenomegaly, fever, wasting, and pancytopenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), from L. donovani/L. infantum, causes hepatosplenomegaly, fever, wasting, and pancytopenia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Congenital toxoplasmosis presents in newborns with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications, and it is not a form of leishmaniasis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary amebic meningoencephalitis is a rapidly fatal Naegleria brain infection after freshwater exposure, not a chronic wasting illness with splenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis destroys nasal and oral mucosa years after a skin ulcer and does not cause massive splenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a localized skin ulcer at the sandfly bite, without fever, wasting, or organomegaly.

questions.stem: Years after a healed skin ulcer, this patient develops progressive destruction of the nasal and oral mucosa. Which form of leishmaniasis is shown?

explanation.summary: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (often L. braziliensis) destroys nasopharyngeal mucosa years after the primary cutaneous lesion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (often L. braziliensis) destroys nasopharyngeal mucosa years after the primary cutaneous lesion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Visceral leishmaniasis infects macrophages of the spleen, liver, and marrow, causing fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia rather than mucosal destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is the initial localized skin ulcer; the late spread to destroy nasal and oral mucosa defines the mucocutaneous form.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis can destroy the nasal septum, but it is an ANCA-associated vasculitis that also involves the lungs and kidneys, without a prior parasitic skin ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lepromatous leprosy can cause nasal collapse but with diffuse skin infiltration, nodules, and nerve involvement, not a previously healed ulcer followed by mucosal destruction.

questions.stem: This life-cycle diagram shows an organism entering the host through the nasal passage after freshwater exposure. By what route does it reach the brain?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Retrograde travel up the spinal cord

choices.label: C
choices.text: Across the blood-brain barrier from the gut

choices.label: D
choices.text: Via cranial nerve VII from the middle ear

explanation.summary: N. fowleri ascends the olfactory nerve and crosses the cribriform plate to cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: N. fowleri ascends the olfactory nerve and crosses the cribriform plate to cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Naegleria does not seed the brain hematogenously from the lungs; it enters through the nasal mucosa and climbs directly along olfactory nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The ameba does not travel up the spinal cord; it reaches the frontal lobes through the cribriform plate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Naegleria infection is not acquired by ingestion, and it does not cross the blood-brain barrier from the gut.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The facial nerve is not the portal; Naegleria enters through the nose, not the middle ear, and follows olfactory fibers.

questions.stem: In this life cycle, which animal serves as the definitive host where sexual reproduction and oocyst shedding occur?

explanation.summary: Felids are the definitive host of T. gondii and shed oocysts in feces; humans are intermediate hosts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Felids are the definitive host of T. gondii and shed oocysts in feces; humans are intermediate hosts.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Humans are intermediate hosts that harbor tachyzoites and tissue cysts but do not shed oocysts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cattle and other livestock are intermediate hosts whose undercooked meat can transmit tissue cysts, but sexual reproduction occurs only in felids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Female sandflies are vectors for Leishmania, not part of the Toxoplasma life cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Freshwater snails are intermediate hosts for schistosomes and other flukes, not for Toxoplasma.

questions.stem: This schematic shows a parasite adhering to and invading a host cell, replicating intracellularly, then triggering egress and cell lysis. Which rapidly dividing form of Toxoplasma is depicted?

explanation.summary: The invasive, rapidly replicating form that lyses host cells during acute infection is the tachyzoite; bradyzoites are the latent cyst form.
explanation.whyCorrect: The invasive, rapidly replicating form that lyses host cells during acute infection is the tachyzoite; bradyzoites are the latent cyst form.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Promastigotes are the flagellated forms of Leishmania found in the sandfly gut, not a Toxoplasma stage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oocysts are environmentally resistant forms shed in cat feces, not the intracellular form that replicates and lyses host cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bradyzoites are slowly dividing forms within latent tissue cysts that do not cause rapid cell lysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Amastigotes are the intracellular forms of Leishmania and Trypanosoma cruzi, not Toxoplasma.
